citation.sourceDocument: USDA FNA SNAP FY 2027 Cost-of-Living Adjustments (48 contiguous states and DC), maximum and minimum allotments and deductions, effective Oct 1, 2026
citation.sourceNote: SNAP runs on the FEDERAL FISCAL year, not the calendar year, so these figures are effective October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027 — the one dataset here whose clock differs from every other. The maximum allotments derive from USDA's Thrifty Food Plan and rise irregularly with household size rather than by a fixed increment, which is why they are stored as a table. Past eight people FY 2027 adds $225 per person for households of nine to seventeen, and then states a flat $3,887 for eighteen or more — less than the $4,091 the increment would give at eighteen, so it is a cap and is stored as one (largeHouseholdAllotment). Through FY 2026 the table had a single "Each Additional Member" row and no cap. The benefit is not the allotment: it is the maximum allotment minus 30% of net income (the expected contribution), floored at a $25 minimum for one- and two-person households. Net income is gross income minus the standard deduction and 20% of earned income. Eligibility runs on two tests, gross income at or below 130% of the poverty line and net income at or below 100%; FNS's FY 2027 limits are the 2026 HHS guidelines this repo already carries ($1,330 net and $1,729 gross for one person). This shard covers the 48 CONTIGUOUS STATES AND DC only; Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands have their own, higher allotments and are not seeded. Omitted: the excess shelter deduction (often the largest deduction a household has, capped at $769 except for elderly or disabled members), the homeless shelter, dependent-care, medical and child-support deductions, the asset limits ($3,000, or $4,750 with a member 60+ or disabled), broad-based categorical eligibility (which many states use to waive the gross-income test), the ABAWD work requirements, and the state options that vary all of this. The figure is an estimate of the maximum a household could receive, not an eligibility determination. Every figure here was read on 2026-10-19 from the COLA index page and checked against FNA's print versions (snap-fy27maximumAllotments-deductions.pdf, snap-fy27MinimumAllotments.pdf); the refresh adapter reads all of them. The agency renamed itself the Food and Nutrition Administration on June 1, 2026, and fns.usda.gov now redirects to fna.usda.gov.
